title: Sharing identical items
objectives: Count ways to share identical items with stars and bars.
Tell when items are identical and when they are distinguishable.

screens.prose: A jar holds 5 identical sweets. You share all of them among Amy, Ben and Cal. Ben gets none, and Amy gets one more than Cal.
screens.question: Drag the sweets to share them that way.

hints.text: Amy and Cal share all 5 sweets between them.
Try giving Cal 2.
Cal 2 and Amy 3 makes 5, and 3 is one more than 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use all 5 sweets, give Ben none, and give Amy one more than Cal.

byKey.count-amy: Amy should have one more than Cal, with all 5 sweets shared between those two.
byKey.count-cal: Cal should have one fewer than Amy, with all 5 sweets shared between those two.

explain.text: You gave Amy 3, Ben 0 and Cal 2. The sweets are identical, so only the numbers matter. Written in a row, it reads ●●● | | ●●: two bars cut the sweets into three groups.

screens.prose: Every sharing of 5 sweets among 3 children is a row of 7 places: 5 sweets and 2 bars. Sweets before the first bar go to Amy, between the bars to Ben, after the second bar to Cal.

state.caption: Tap two places to be bars; the rest are sweets

screens.question: Tap the 2 places for the bars that give Amy 0, Ben 4 and Cal 1.

hints.text: Amy gets nothing, so where must the first bar go?
The first bar comes before any sweet.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the sweets before, between and after your two bars.

byKey.c2: A bar at place 2 leaves a sweet before it, so Amy would get 1.
byKey.c5: A bar at place 5 leaves Ben 3 sweets. He needs 4.
byKey.c7: A bar at the end leaves Cal nothing. He needs 1.

explain.text: Bars at places 1 and 6 give | ●●●● | ●. Each choice of 2 bar places out of 7 is exactly one sharing. So counting sharings means counting ways to place the bars.

screens.prose: This way of coding a sharing is called **stars and bars**. The row below is Amy 3, Ben 0, Cal 2. Any 2 of the 7 places can hold the bars.
screens.question: How many ways can the 5 sweets be shared among the 3 children?

hints.text: A sharing is fixed once you know where the 2 bars go.
Choose 2 places out of 7 for the bars. The two bars look alike.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the ways to choose 2 of the 7 places for the bars.

byKey.distinct: That is $3^5$: each sweet picks a child. It counts sweets as different, but they are identical.
byKey.five-places: You chose 2 of 5 places. The row has 7 places: 5 sweets and 2 bars.
byKey.ordered-bars: You counted the bars in order. The bars look alike, so halve it.

explain.text: A sharing is a choice of 2 bar places out of 7, so there are $\binom{7}{2} = 21$. Empty shares are allowed: bars side by side give Ben nothing. Because the sweets are identical, swapping two of them changes nothing.

screens.prose: Now the jar holds 8 identical sweets for the same 3 children. One possible row is drawn: Amy 2, Ben 5, Cal 1.
screens.question: How many ways can the 8 sweets be shared?

hints.text: How many places does the row have?
8 stars and 2 bars make 10 places.
Choose 2 of 10 for the bars: $\tfrac{10 \times 9}{2}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the places in the row, then choose 2 for the bars.

byKey.distinct: That is $3^8$, which treats the sweets as different. They are identical.
byKey.eight-places: You chose 2 of 8 places. The bars take places too: 10 in all.
byKey.ordered-bars: You counted the bars in order. They look alike, so halve it.
byKey.nine-places: You used 9 places. There are 8 stars and 2 bars, so 10.

explain.text: The row has $8 + 2 = 10$ places, and any 2 can be bars. So there are $\binom{10}{2} = 45$ sharings. In general, $n$ stars and $k - 1$ bars give $\binom{n + k - 1}{k - 1}$.

screens.prose: Back to 5 sweets and 3 children, but now each child must get at least one. Line up the 5 stars. The bars must go in the gaps between stars, at most one per gap.
screens.question: How many sharings give every child at least one sweet?

hints.text: How many gaps between the stars could take a bar?
There are 4 gaps, at places 2, 4, 6 and 8.
Choose 2 of the 4 gaps: $\binom{4}{2} = 6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose 2 of the 4 gaps for the bars.

byKey.any: That allows empty shares. Each child needs at least one sweet.
byKey.stars: You chose 2 of the 5 stars. Bars go in the 4 gaps between stars.
byKey.children: You counted the children. Count the ways to choose 2 gaps of 4.

explain.text: One bar per gap keeps every group non-empty, so choose 2 of the 4 gaps: $\binom{4}{2} = 6$. Another view: hand one sweet to each child first, then share the other 2 freely. That is $\binom{2+2}{2} = 6$ again.

screens.prose: A fund has 12 identical lots to place, and only one broker. With $k = 1$ child there are $k - 1 = 0$ bars.
screens.question: How many ways can the 12 lots be shared with one broker?

hints.text: Can the single broker get anything other than all 12?
With no bars, the row is fixed.
The formula gives $\binom{12 + 1 - 1}{0} = \binom{12}{0} = 1$.

feedback.correct: One way: everything to the one broker.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With one broker, every lot must go to that broker.

byKey.lots: You counted the lots. They are identical, and all must go to the one broker: one sharing.
byKey.places: You counted places for a bar. With one broker there are no bars to place.
byKey.none: There is a sharing: the broker gets all 12. That is one way, not none.

explain.text: With one broker, all 12 lots go to that broker, so there is exactly one sharing. The formula agrees: $\binom{12}{0} = 1$, choosing no places for no bars. Edge cases like this are good tests of a formula.

screens.prose: Sam shares 5 identical £1 coins among Amy, Ben and Cal, empty shares allowed. Sam says each coin picks one of 3 children, so there are $3^5 = 243$ ways.
screens.question: How many different sharings are there?

options.why: That is Sam's count. It treats coin 1 to Amy and coin 2 to Ben as different from the swap. Identical coins make those the same.
That is $5^3$, as if each child picks a number from 5. The amounts must also add to 5.
That is $\binom{5}{2}$, bars among the coins only. The bars need places of their own: 7 in all.

hints.text: Does it matter which £1 coin Amy gets?
Only the amounts each child gets matter: Amy 2, Ben 2, Cal 1 is one sharing.
Use stars and bars: 5 stars, 2 bars, $\binom{7}{2}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only the number of coins each child gets matters.

byKey.distinct: That is Sam's count. It treats coin 1 to Amy and coin 2 to Ben as different from the swap. Identical coins make those the same.

explain.text: $3^5 = 243$ counts coins that can be told apart, such as 5 different bonds. With identical coins, many of those 243 collapse to the same amounts. Counting amounts with stars and bars gives $\binom{7}{2} = 21$.

canvas.caption: Amy 2, Ben 2, Cal 1 is one sharing, whichever coins go where

screens.prose: Each time, you placed $k - 1$ bars among $n$ identical stars. So $n$ identical items go to $k$ people in $$\binom{n + k - 1}{k - 1} \text{ ways.}$$ If everyone must get at least one, the bars go in the $n - 1$ gaps: $$\binom{n - 1}{k - 1} \text{ ways.}$$
screens.question: How many ways can 6 identical sweets go to 4 children, empty shares allowed?

options.why: That treats the sweets as different. Identical sweets need stars and bars.
You chose 4 places, one per child. Four children need only 3 bars.
That makes every child get at least one. Here empty shares are allowed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $n = 6$ stars and $k - 1 = 3$ bars.

explain.text: Six stars and three bars make 9 places, and any 3 can be bars. So there are $\binom{9}{3} = 84$ sharings. With at least one each it would be $\binom{5}{3} = 10$.

screens.prose: For 3 children the count is $\binom{n+2}{2}$, the ways to place 2 bars among $n + 2$ places. Use $\binom{m}{2} = \tfrac{m(m-1)}{2}$, the ordered pairs halved, with $m = n + 2$: $$\binom{n+2}{2} = \frac{(n+2)(n+2-1)}{2}$$
screens.question: Simplify: write the number of sharings among 3 children in terms of $n$.

hints.text: Simplify $n + 2 - 1$ first.
So the count is $(n+2)(n+1)$ over 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Replace $n + 2 - 1$ by $n + 1$ and keep the division by 2.

byKey.distinct: $3^n$ treats the items as different. Identical items give the stars and bars count.
byKey.no-half: You kept the ordered pairs of bar places. The bars look alike, so divide by 2.
byKey.n-places: That places the bars among $n$ places only. The bars add 2 places, so use $n + 2$.

explain.text: $n + 2 - 1 = n + 1$, so the count is $\tfrac{(n+2)(n+1)}{2}$. Check: $n = 5$ gives $\tfrac{7 \times 6}{2} = 21$ and $n = 8$ gives 45, your counts. It grows like $\tfrac{n^2}{2}$, far slower than $3^n$.

screens.prose: You split £10,000 across 4 funds in whole £1,000 units. A fund may get nothing. Only the amount in each fund matters, so the units are identical.
screens.question: How many different allocations are possible?

hints.text: How many stars, and how many bars?
10 units are the stars; 4 funds need 3 bars.
Choose 3 of 13 places: $\binom{13}{3} = \tfrac{13 \times 12 \times 11}{6}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use 10 stars and 3 bars, and choose the bar places.

byKey.distinct: That is $4^{10}$, which treats each £1,000 unit as different. Only the amounts matter.
byKey.no-bar-places: You chose 3 of 10 places. The 3 bars need places too: 13 in all.
byKey.k-bars: You chose 4 bar places out of 13. Four funds need only 3 bars to separate them.
byKey.at-least-one: That gives every fund at least £1,000. Here a fund may get nothing.

explain.text: Ten £1,000 units are stars and 3 bars split them into 4 funds. Choosing 3 of the 13 places gives $\binom{13}{3} = 286$ allocations. A grid search over these weights would test 286 portfolios, not a million.

ideas: A sharing of $n$ identical items among $k$ people is a row of $n$ stars and $k - 1$ bars.
Choosing the bar places gives $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$; with at least one each, bars go in the $n-1$ gaps: $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$.
With $k = 1$ there are no bars and one way. Distinguishable items use $k^n$ instead.

formula.name: Stars and bars
formula.note: $n$ identical items, $k$ people, empty shares allowed.

summary.trap: $k^n$ lets each item pick a person, which counts items as different. Identical items need stars and bars.

quiz.prose: A desk allocates 20 identical lots across 5 brokers. A broker may get none.
quiz.question: How many allocations are possible?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\binom{n + k - 1}{k - 1}$ with $n = 20$ and $k = 5$.

byKey.no-bar-places: You chose 4 of 20 places. The bars add 4 places: 24 in all.
byKey.k-bars: You chose 5 bar places. Five brokers need only 4 bars.
byKey.at-least-one: That gives every broker at least one lot. Here a broker may get none.

explain.text: The 20 lots are stars and 4 bars split them among 5 brokers. That is $\binom{24}{4} = 10{,}626$ allocations. With at least one lot each it would be $\binom{19}{4} = 3{,}876$.

quiz.prose: Seven identical client orders are routed to 3 desks. Every desk must get at least one order.
quiz.question: How many routings are possible?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the 2 bars in the 6 gaps between the 7 orders.

byKey.empty-allowed: That allows a desk with nothing. Each desk needs at least one order.
byKey.seven-gaps: 7 stars have 6 gaps between them, not 7.

explain.text: Seven stars have 6 gaps between them. Two bars in different gaps give every desk at least one order. So there are $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ routings.

quiz.prose: Now the items are different: 5 different bonds go into 3 portfolios, and a portfolio may stay empty.
quiz.question: How many assignments are possible?

options.why: Stars and bars counts identical items. Different bonds can be told apart, so who gets which bond matters.
You let each portfolio pick a bond. Each bond picks a portfolio: 3 choices, 5 times.

feedback.correct: Each bond picks one of 3 portfolios.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each of the 5 bonds is a stage with 3 choices.

explain.text: Each of the 5 different bonds goes to one of 3 portfolios, so the multiplication rule gives $3^5 = 243$. Stars and bars is for identical items, where only the amounts matter.

quiz.prose: Count the solutions of $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4 = 3$, where each $x_i$ is a whole number 0 or more.
quiz.question: How many solutions are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each $x_i$ is a child's share of 3 identical stars.

byKey.three-bars-wrong: That is $\binom{4}{3}$, bars among the 4 variables. Use 3 stars and 3 bars: 6 places.
byKey.distinct: That is $4^3$, as if the 3 units were different. They are identical.
byKey.four-bars: You chose 4 bar places, one per variable. Four variables need only 3 bars: $\binom{6}{3}$.

explain.text: Each solution shares 3 identical units among 4 variables. Stars and bars: 3 stars and 3 bars, so $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ solutions. For example, $(1, 0, 2, 0)$ is ● | | ●● |.
